explain: With runtime n and two pointers that may overlap, vectorizing needs a runtime overlap check. The very-cheap model used at -O2 refuses any runtime alias check (and, before GCC 15, any loop needing a scalar epilogue); -O3's dynamic model accepts them. restrict (plus a known trip count on GCC 14 and older) can make -O2 vectorize it.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached
question: You build a CLI tool on a new workstation with `-O2 -march=native` and publish the binary for all Linux x86-64 users. What is the main risk?
options: It runs slower on older CPUs
It produces different numeric results on AMD
It may use instructions older CPUs lack, so it fails to run there
Nothing, -march only affects scheduling
explain: -march=native enables every extension of the build machine, and GCC's manual warns the result might not run elsewhere. For a distributed binary use the default target, a psABI level like x86-64-v2 or v3 that you document, or runtime dispatch (ship several versions of the hot code and pick one at startup from the CPU's features). -mtune changes scheduling only.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: Coordinates: grounding a click and scaling it to the real display
question: Clicks land in the right area but often miss very small targets. Scaling is verified correct. Which fix matches the docs' guidance?
options: Send the screenshot at a higher resolution than the image limit so the API keeps detail
Switch the aspect ratio of the screenshot to 1:1 so the model counts pixels more easily
Keep zoom enabled so the model can inspect the region at full resolution, and keep the aspect ratio when resizing
Retry each click three times at random offsets of a few pixels
explain: The docs attribute right-area misses to tiny targets, detail lost when downscaling a large source, or distorted aspect ratio, and suggest zoom, cropping or capturing at lower DPI (dots per inch), and preserving aspect ratio. Oversized images are rejected, not kept. Random retries can click the wrong thing.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Why a concurrent test can pass a million times and still be wrong
question: Your lock-free queue test passed 50,000 times on an x86 laptop. A teammate says it is now safe to ship to Arm servers. What is the strongest objection?
options: 50,000 runs is too few; 5 million runs would be enough
x86 hardware keeps more orderings than Arm, so a missing Release or Acquire may simply be invisible there and still break on Arm
The test should have been run in debug mode instead of release mode
Lock-free code cannot be tested at all, only proven
explain: Running more often only samples more schedules of the same hardware memory model. Weak-ordering bugs that x86's stronger hardware ordering hides have probability zero there, so no count of x86 runs covers them. A tool that models the language memory model, like loom, can explore those executions.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: Choosing and running loom and ThreadSanitizer in a real project
question: A CI job runs your C++ service's integration tests under `-fsanitize=thread` and reports nothing for months. Which statement is justified?
options: The service is free of data races
TSan is misconfigured, since every large program has races
The service cannot deadlock
No data race occurred, unordered by happens-before, on the code paths and synchronization these tests exercised
explain: TSan is a dynamic detector: it is precise about what it saw but blind to paths that never ran and to races hidden by incidental synchronization in this run. Clean reports are evidence about the executed paths only.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: iCT, sCM, LCM and the other few-step distillers
question: You need a one-step text-to-image model and have no budget for training a new diffusion model, but you do have a strong pretrained latent diffusion model with classifier-free guidance. Which approach fits best?
options: Latent consistency distillation (LCM) or adversarial diffusion distillation from that model
Consistency training from scratch on pixels
Progressive distillation from 8192 steps in pixel space
Plain L2 regression from noise to random images
explain: LCM and ADD both start from an existing latent diffusion teacher and target 1 to 4 steps; LCM distills the guided ODE directly (about 32 A100 hours for its 768x768 model). CT from scratch means training a new model; PD takes many halving stages; noise-to-random-image regression learns the mean.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Why quorum overlap alone is not linearizable, and the fix
question: A Dynamo-style store uses N=3, W=2, R=2 with last-write-wins timestamps and no read write-back. Which anomaly can still occur?
options: A read missing a write that completed long ago
Two reads in sequence, the second returning an older value than the first while a write is in flight
A read returning a value that was never written
Writes being lost because W is not equal to N
explain: With W + R greater than N, every completed write is seen by later quorum reads. But during a write that has reached only some replicas, one read can see it and a later read can miss it, exactly the R2 then R3 pattern. ABD's write-back closes that gap.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Virtual nodes: many tokens per server smooth out the load
question: You run 20 nodes with 1 token each and see one node at 3x average load. Which change reduces the spread of per-node load most directly?
options: Switch the key hash from MD5 to a faster hash
Give each node about 100 tokens (virtual nodes)
Add 5 more nodes with 1 token each
Replicate every key to 3 nodes
explain: Spread comes from uneven arc sizes. With T tokens per node the relative spread falls roughly like 1/sqrt(T), so 100 tokens cuts it to around 10%. A different hash function does not change the geometry, more single-token nodes stay just as uneven, and replication multiplies storage without evening out arcs.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Decay functions turn distance and recency into smooth scores
question: With gauss on distance, offset 5 km, scale 20 km, decay 0.5: what does a candidate 25 km away score, and what does one 4 km away score?
explain: At 25 km, d = 25 - 5 = 20 = scale, so the score equals decay, 0.5. At 4 km the candidate is inside the offset, d = 0, so the score is 1.0.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
question: X and Y have domain {1,2,3} and the only constraint is X < Y. What does AC-3 leave?
options: X {1,2,3}, Y {1,2,3}, because no value is fixed yet
X {1,2}, Y {1,2,3}, because only the arc (X,Y) is revised
explain: Revising (X,Y) deletes X=3 (no larger Y); revising (Y,X) deletes Y=1 (no smaller X). X=1 is supported by Y=2 or 3, and X=2 by Y=3, so nothing else goes. AC-3 keeps every value that appears in some solution of a single constraint; it does not pick a solution.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: One kernel, many tenants: the container threat model
question: Why is a container escape usually considered easier to find than a VM escape?
options: Container images are public
Containers share the host kernel, whose large system call interface is directly reachable, while a VM's guest talks to a much smaller hypervisor interface
Containers are written in Go
VMs encrypt their memory
explain: A container's processes make system calls straight into the host kernel, so any kernel bug reachable through those calls is a candidate. A VM's kernel is separate; escaping needs a bug in the hypervisor's narrower interface.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Runtime settings that switch the fences off
question: A team says their pod needs `privileged: true` only to change one network setting. What is the better request?
options: Disable seccomp but keep capabilities default
Keep privileged; it is the same thing
Use hostPID instead
Add only the specific capability needed (for example NET_ADMIN) and keep seccomp, AppArmor or SELinux on
explain: The Kubernetes docs advise granting specific capabilities rather than privileged mode, because privileged also removes seccomp and LSM confinement and grants every capability.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Service account tokens and cloud identity for pods
question: Five apps in namespace shop all use the default service account. An admin binds a Role allowing `get secrets` to it so one app can read its config. What changed for the other four?
options: All four can now read Secrets in shop, because they run as the same identity
Only if they mount the Secret
Only pods created after the binding are affected
Nothing, roles are per app
explain: RBAC grants rights to the identity, and all five pods share it. Give each app its own service account so a binding affects only the app that needs it.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Exposed dashboards, kubelets and Docker APIs
question: A self-built cluster's kubelets run with flags only, no config file, and `--anonymous-auth` and `--authorization-mode` are not set. Port 10250 is reachable from the internet. What can an unauthenticated stranger do?
options: Only list pod names
Run commands in containers through the kubelet API, since anonymous requests are allowed and authorization defaults to AlwaysAllow
Nothing, because port 10250 uses TLS
Only read node metrics
explain: The kubelet auth docs give these defaults: anonymous requests accepted, AlwaysAllow authorization. TLS encrypts the connection but does not authenticate the caller. This is the Hildegard entry point.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: A container is a process with a narrowed view
question: A process inside a pid namespace runs the equivalent of kill -TERM 1, aiming at its own init process, which has installed no SIGTERM handler. What happens?
options: The signal is delivered, pid 1 exits, and the kernel SIGKILLs the rest of the namespace
Nothing reaches pid 1: a namespace member may only signal its init process for signals that init handles
The signal is redirected to the host's pid 1
The kernel rejects the call because pid 1 is in another namespace
explain: pid_namespaces(7) says only signals for which the init process has established a handler can be sent to it by other members of the namespace, and that this holds even for privileged processes. It exists to stop a container accidentally killing its own init. SIGKILL and SIGSTOP are forced through only when sent from an ancestor namespace.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: Probes, Services and DNS: liveness is not readiness
question: An application takes 40 s to warm its caches. Its only probe is a liveness probe with initialDelaySeconds 10, periodSeconds 5 and failureThreshold 3. What do you observe?
options: The pod becomes Ready at 40 s, because liveness failures only affect traffic
The container is restarted at about 20 s and keeps restarting, because the budget is 10 + 3 x 5 = 25 s
The pod stays Pending until the probe succeeds
Nothing: the kubelet waits for a first success before it starts counting failures
explain: Probes at 10, 15 and 20 seconds all fail, which reaches failureThreshold, so the kubelet restarts the container and the clock starts over. The fix is a startup probe on the same endpoint: periodSeconds 10 with failureThreshold 30 allows 300 s, succeeds at 40 s, and only then lets liveness and readiness begin.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: A five-turn session: diffs, state and generated queries
question: Which turn in the session is a replace rather than an add?
options: T2 now only remote ones
T3 actually make it staff level
T4 drop the salary limit
T1 the first search
explain: Level already held senior and changes to staff, so it is a replace. T2 fills a null slot (add), T4 empties a slot (remove), and T1 is four adds onto an empty state.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Poking the chain: truncate it, break it, reword it
question: You suspect a model hides information in its word choices. Which intervention tests this most directly, and what result would support your suspicion?
options: Filler tokens; accuracy rises with more dots
Early answering; the answer is fixed at step 0
Adding mistakes; answers ignore the mistake
Paraphrasing; accuracy drops when the same content is reworded
explain: Encoded reasoning lives in the exact phrasing, so rewording the content while keeping its meaning should destroy it and cost accuracy. Lanham et al. saw no such drop. Filler tokens test hidden compute, not hidden encoding; the other two test post-hoc reasoning.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Building and scoring a CoT monitor
question: A monitor flags 2% of clean runs and catches 90% of hacks. Hacks occur in 0.5% of runs. About what share of flags are real hacks?
options: About 18%
About 90%
About 2%
About 50%
explain: precision = 0.005 x 0.9 / (0.005 x 0.9 + 0.995 x 0.02) = 0.0045 / (0.0045 + 0.0199) = 0.184. 90% is recall, not precision. At this base rate, false alarms outnumber real hacks more than 4 to 1.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Pinned host memory: the precondition for overlap
question: On which system does switching from pageable to pinned host memory help least, and why?
options: The laptop, because its link is slower so the copy dominates either way
Neither; the ratio is a property of the PCIe generation, not the host
The desktop, because a faster GPU hides the staging copy behind the kernel
The desktop, because its CPU runs the driver's staging memcpy fast enough that staging was not the bottleneck
explain: Pageable transfers were 5.369 GB/s on the desktop against 2.308 GB/s on the laptop, so the desktop's staging memcpy was already near link speed and pinning only added 1.15x there, against 2.50x on the laptop. The bottleneck being removed is host-side, which is why the benefit is a property of the host.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: A worked pipeline: four chunks, and the copy-bound crossover
question: Same pipeline, but you move to a link that is twice as fast, so H2D per chunk drops from 4.00 to 2.00 ms and D2H to 0.125 ms. What is the new 4-chunk time?
options: 14.13 ms, half of before
24.00 ms, the kernel total exactly
26.13 ms, and the speedup over the new serial time drops to 1.24x
28.25 ms, unchanged, because the kernel was already the bottleneck
explain: Makespan is sum + (n-1) x max = (2.00 + 6.00 + 0.125) + 3 x 6.00 = 26.13 ms. New serial time is 4 x 8.125 = 32.50 ms, so the speedup from overlap falls to 1.24x. Faster links make the absolute time better and the overlap win smaller, because there is less copy time left to hide.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Host memory as a tier: unified memory, zero-copy and offloading
question: A kernel reads a 4 KB block of parameters exactly once per launch, with coalesced loads, and the CPU rewrites the block between launches. Which home fits best?
options: Mapped pinned host memory: each byte crosses the link once, inside the kernel, with no separate copy to schedule
Managed memory with no hints, so pages migrate on demand every launch
Pageable malloc memory passed to cudaMemcpyAsync on a side stream
Copy it once at startup and never again
explain: The best practices guide's condition for zero-copy is data read or written only once with coalesced accesses, which this is. Managed memory would fault and migrate pages back and forth every launch. A pageable source makes cudaMemcpyAsync synchronous. Copying once is wrong because the CPU changes the data every launch.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Packing the pair: special tokens, segments and the 512-token limit
question: A query is 20 tokens and a passage is 600 tokens. Using a BERT tokenizer with max_length 512 and truncation=True, how many passage tokens remain?
explain: Three special tokens ([CLS] and two [SEP]) plus 20 query tokens use 23 positions, leaving 512 - 23 = 489 for the passage. longest_first trims the longer side, which is the passage.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
question: In the listwise softmax view, which candidate in our group receives the largest gradient pushing its score down?
options: The easy negative at -4.0
The positive at 2.0
The hard negative at 1.5
All negatives receive equal gradient
explain: For softmax cross-entropy the gradient on each negative's logit is its probability: 0.331 for z = 1.5, 0.122 for 0.5 and 0.001 for the easy one. The loss focuses on whichever negatives currently compete with the positive.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: What cryptography promises, and to whom
question: By Kerckhoffs's principle, which of these should be treated as secret?
options: The cipher's name
The source code of the encryption routine
The key
The message format
explain: Only the key. Everything else should be assumed known to the attacker, because in practice it eventually is.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Block ciphers: what AES actually does to 16 bytes
question: A message is exactly 32 bytes long. How many bytes does it occupy after PKCS7 padding for AES?
explain: Already a multiple of 16, so a full block of padding (sixteen 0x10 bytes) is added: 48 bytes. This keeps unpadding unambiguous.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: When hashes break: MD5, Flame and the SHA-1 collision
question: A team stores SHA-1 hashes of uploaded files to detect duplicates and auto-merge "identical" uploads from different users. What is the risk?
options: None, SHA-1 is only weak for passwords
SHA-1 hashes are too long to store
An attacker can upload a harmless file and a harmful one with the same SHA-1, and the system will treat them as the same file
Duplicate detection needs encryption
explain: Users choose the inputs, so collision resistance is needed. SHAttered showed two different PDFs with one SHA-1. Use SHA-256.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Diffie-Hellman: agreeing on a secret in public
question: Why does TLS sign the Diffie-Hellman values instead of just exchanging them?
options: To make the exchange faster
Signatures encrypt the shared secret
Plain DH cannot tell Bob from a man in the middle; the signature proves the server's identity
DH values are too short without a signature
explain: DH guarantees a shared secret with whoever answered. Authentication (certificate plus signature) ensures that whoever answered is the real server.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Sound primitives, broken systems: how crypto use fails
question: According to Lazar and colleagues' study of 269 crypto CVEs from 2011 to 2014, where did most of the bugs sit?
options: In the cryptographic primitives such as AES
In protocol implementations such as TLS libraries
In applications calling crypto libraries incorrectly
Spread evenly across the three layers
explain: 223 of 269 were application bugs (83%), such as hard-coded keys, plaintext storage, weak seeds and skipped certificate checks. Primitive bugs were 7. That is why this course focuses on how crypto is used.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Nonce budgets for AEAD: counters, random nonces, XChaCha, GCM-SIV
question: Your team cannot guarantee nonce uniqueness because several independent writers share one key and keep no shared state. Which choice fits best?
options: AES-GCM with a fixed nonce, since it is fast
AES-CTR with an HMAC
AES-GCM-SIV or XChaCha20-Poly1305 with random nonces
AES-ECB, which needs no nonce
explain: RFC 8452 suggests AES-GCM-SIV wherever nonce uniqueness cannot be guaranteed, including multiple encryptors sharing a key, and XChaCha20's 192-bit random nonces make collisions negligible. ECB leaks patterns, and a fixed GCM nonce is the exact failure to avoid.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Randomness in practice: weak, shared and first-boot keys
question: Why did different RSA keys in the Ps and Qs study become breakable even though no two keys were identical?
options: They used tiny primes
The devices published their private keys
They used MD5 in the certificate
Pairs of moduli shared one prime factor because of low entropy at generation, and a greatest common divisor reveals that shared prime
explain: Two moduli n1 = p q1 and n2 = p q2 built from the same p look unrelated, but their greatest common divisor is p, a cheap computation that factors both. The cause was poor randomness during key generation on embedded devices.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Why a fast GEMM is a hierarchy of tiles
question: A kernel uses 128x128 CTA tiles in FP16 and is still memory bound. Which change raises the tile's arithmetic intensity against global memory?
options: Growing the tile to 256x128
Doubling bK from 32 to 64 while keeping 128x128
Launching more threads per CTA with the same tile
Switching the inputs from FP16 to FP32
explain: Intensity is 2 bM bN / ((bM + bN) s). bK cancels out, thread count does not appear, and FP32 doubles s, halving intensity. 256x128 raises it from 64 to about 85 FLOP per byte, as long as shared memory and registers can hold it.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: Hopper mainloops: TMA, stages and warp specialization
question: A 128x256x64 FP16 tile on SM90 with no epilogue carveout. Using the builder's formula, how many stages fit?
explain: One stage is (128 + 256) x 64 x 2 = 49152 bytes, plus 16 bytes of barriers: 49168. 232448 / 49168 = 4.7, so 4 stages. The wider tile buys reuse at the price of pipeline depth.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
question: Using Pond's model (local 85 ns, 8-socket pool 155 ns), what is the average miss latency if 25% of misses go to the pool?
options: 120 ns
155 ns
explain: 85 + 0.25 x (155 - 85) = 85 + 17.5 = 102.5 ns. 120 ns would be f = 0.5; 155 ns is all misses on CXL.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
question: Which of these is an ethics question rather than a legal or authorisation question?
options: Does section 1 of the Computer Misuse Act cover this scan?
Did the client sign the rules of engagement?
Should we publish a technique that is legal and authorised but would let others hurt patients before hospitals can patch?
Is the target address inside the agreed range?
explain: The first is law, the second and fourth are authorisation. Whether to publish a lawful finding, and when, turns on the harm it could do to people outside the contract, which is the subject of professional ethics codes and of coordinated disclosure.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: The UK Computer Misuse Act, section by section
question: Which CMA section is most directly concerned with a DDoS attack that takes a council's website offline for an afternoon?
options: Section 3
Section 1
Section 3A
Section 17
explain: Section 3 covers unauthorised acts intended to impair, or reckless as to impairing, a computer's operation or access to data. The CPS guidance names DDoS and notes impairment can be temporary. Section 1 needs an intent to secure access; section 17 is definitions.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Export controls: Wassenaar and 'intrusion software'
question: Why did BIS add NSO Group and Candiru to the Entity List in November 2021?
options: They failed to patch their own systems
They exported encryption without a licence
They published vulnerability research
Investigative information showed they developed and supplied spyware that foreign governments used to target officials, journalists, activists and others
explain: The Federal Register notice gives that reason under EAR section 744.11. It is an example of export law reaching the market for offensive capability rather than the research that finds bugs.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Cover-ups and whistleblowing: Uber's CSO and Twitter's security lead
question: According to Zatko's Senate testimony, what did they do before going to government agencies and regulators?
options: Repeatedly disclosed the security failures to the highest levels of the company
Published Twitter's source code
Sold the information to a journalist
Nothing; they went to regulators first
explain: The written testimony says it was only after internal reports went unheeded that disclosures were submitted to government agencies and regulators. That ordering is what most whistleblowing laws and codes expect.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: The domain-weight update, step by step
question: In the update, why are weights multiplied by exp(eta x excess) rather than having eta x excess added to them?
options: Addition would be slower to compute on accelerators
Exponentials make the excess loss smaller
Multiplying keeps weights positive and, after renormalizing, a valid probability vector; adding could push weights negative
explain: Exponentiated gradient ascent is the standard update on the probability simplex. Multiplicative updates never cross zero, and renormalization restores the sum to 1.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Fitting a mixing law: RegMix, data mixing laws, judging a mixture
question: Aioli found DoReMi 6.9 perplexity points worse than uniform (stratified) weights in one data setting. What did its analysis blame?
options: DoReMi's implicit mixing law has a reasonable form, but its parameters were set inaccurately for that data
Stratified sampling secretly uses more compute
The 160M models were too small for any method to work
DoReMi was run without a reference model
explain: Aioli writes every method as minimizing average loss under a method-specific mixing law. The laws fit real training runs well, but the parameter values the methods use differ from the best-fit ones, and that gap tracked their losses against stratified sampling.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Curation inside a domain: quality filters from phi-1 to FineWeb-Edu
question: After filtering removes 90% of your web domain, should you reuse the domain weights DoReMi produced before filtering?
options: No, filtering changes the domain's size, difficulty and excess losses, so the weights should be recomputed
Yes, weights are a property of the domain's name
Yes, as long as the tokenizer is unchanged
explain: DoReMi's weights come from per-domain excess losses measured on the actual data. A filtered domain is different data with a different loss profile, and a 90% smaller domain may now be repeated many times at the old weight.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Choosing a layout: hot/cold splits, ECS chunks and columnar data
question: Your ECS component `Transform` is read by rendering every frame, but you also add and remove a `Stunned` marker component on thousands of entities per second. Using Bevy's storage options, which setup fits?
options: Both as SparseSet, since additions are frequent
Transform as Table (default) for fast iteration, Stunned as SparseSet for cheap add and remove
Both as Table, because Table is always faster
Transform as SparseSet, Stunned as Table
explain: Table storage gives cache-friendly iteration but costs more on add and remove; SparseSet is the reverse. Transform is iterated constantly and rarely added, Stunned churns constantly, so each gets the storage that matches its access pattern.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Classification: levels, impact and the high-water mark
question: Under Executive Order 13526, what distinguishes Secret from Confidential?
options: The expected damage from disclosure: serious damage for Secret, damage for Confidential
Secret covers foreign information only
Who wrote the document
Secret information can never be declassified
explain: The three levels are defined by the damage unauthorised disclosure could reasonably be expected to cause to national security: exceptionally grave (Top Secret), serious (Secret), damage (Confidential). Declassification dates apply to all levels.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Database security I: accounts, grants, views and the revoke trap
question: The app connects with a role that has SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE on `orders` but no DELETE and no DDL. An attacker finds SQL injection in the app. What do these grants limit?
options: Nothing: injection bypasses database permissions
The attacker can read only the masked view
The attacker can still read and change orders through the app's rights, but cannot delete rows or drop tables
Injection is impossible because of the grants
explain: Injected SQL runs with the application's database role, so it gets exactly the app's rights: still serious (read and modify), but no DELETE or DROP. Grants limit damage; parameterised queries prevent the injection itself.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Insider risk: definitions, the Tesla files and running a programme
question: Under CISA's definitions, which of these is an insider threat?
options: An external attacker scanning the company's VPN
A contractor with valid access who mistakenly emails a customer file to the wrong external address
A phishing email arriving from outside
A public vulnerability report about the company's product
explain: An insider is anyone who has or had authorised access; the threat can be unintentional. A contractor is a third-party insider, and a misdirected email is CISA's own example of an accidental insider threat. The others are external events.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: An alarm nobody should trip: why deception detects
question: A behaviour rule and a decoy file both have some false positives. Why can the decoy still be the better alert?
options: Decoys never produce false positives, so precision is always 100%
Its alert volume is tiny because only things that touch it are judged, so each alert can be investigated fully
Decoys detect every intrusion, so recall is perfect
Decoy alerts are encrypted, so attackers cannot suppress them
explain: Accidental touches do happen (option A is wrong), and a decoy only fires if the intruder touches it (option C is wrong). Its value is a very small, mostly meaningful stream of alerts.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: DNS canaries: tripwires that escape locked-down networks
question: A DNS canary alert shows source address 8.8.8.8 (a public resolver). What does that tell you?
options: The attacker is at Google
The token's hostname was resolved through that public resolver; the host that asked is elsewhere, and your resolver or egress logs must identify it
The alert is a false positive because public resolvers never forward
The attacker used DNS over HTTPS, which cannot be detected
explain: Authoritative servers see the last resolver in the chain, not the client. Use your own DNS logs (or firewall logs if the host went straight to 8.8.8.8) to find the asker.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Placement and the deception story: where decoys earn their keep
question: You have budget for ten decoys. Which deployment is likely to detect more intruders?
options: Ten identical decoys named honeypot01 to honeypot10 in an unused subnet
Decoys named like real servers in the busiest server subnets, with breadcrumbs (saved connections, script credentials) on admin hosts pointing to them
Ten decoys on the Internet edge
One decoy with ten times the logging
explain: Intruders follow names and pointers. Decoys that fit the environment and are linked from places intruders search sit on the attack path; isolated, obviously named decoys do not.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Where a GPU inference stack loses bitwise equality
question: cuBLAS promises the same bit-wise results at every run on GPUs with the same architecture and the same number of SMs. Which of these breaks that promise, by the same document?
options: Calling the identical GEMM twice back to back in one stream.
Upgrading the CUDA toolkit, or running several CUDA streams that share one cuBLAS handle.
Passing the same matrices from pinned rather than pageable host memory.
Writing the result into a different output buffer.
explain: The guarantee is scoped to one toolkit version and is void across versions because implementations change. cuBLAS also states that it no longer holds when multiple CUDA streams are active, because workspace selection among concurrent streams can pick different internal implementations. Host memory kind and output buffer address are not part of the scope.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Beyond one GPU and one dtype: collectives, MoE routing and precision
question: With batch-invariant kernels on, your greedy equivalence test passes at TP 1 and fails at TP 2 on the same GPUs. What is the most likely cause?
options: At TP 2 the row-parallel layers add partial sums through an all-reduce, a different reduction tree from TP 1, so the logits move in their last bits.
Batch-invariant kernels are disabled when more than one GPU is used.
The KV cache is shared between the two GPUs and one of them reads stale entries.
TP 2 halves the batch size seen by each GPU, which changes the sampler's seed.
explain: Batch invariance pins each kernel's order for a given shape. Splitting K across two GPUs and summing with a collective is a different parenthesisation, so TP size is part of the numerics; compare at the same TP and pin the collective (a fixed-order all-reduce, or NCCL_ALGO). Nothing about TP changes a seed, and stale cache reads would be a real bug with a much larger signature.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Inside the simulator: one thread, one seed, simulated time
question: A replica computes its election deadline as `time.time() + random_timeout()`, using Python's real clock, while everything else goes through the simulator. What breaks?
options: Nothing: the timeout value still comes from the seeded generator
Replay: the deadline now depends on wall-clock time, so the same seed can schedule different events
Only performance: real clock reads are slower than simulated ones
Safety of the protocol in production
explain: Wall-clock time differs between runs and is unrelated to simulated time, so the deadline, and every event that depends on it, changes from run to run. One leak like this destroys reproducibility for the whole simulation. All time must come from the simulated clock.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud
question: A company locks down its cloud console with MFA and short sessions, but its deploy pipeline holds a long-lived admin key. Where should an attacker aim?
options: At the console, because it holds the most permissions
At the pipeline: anyone who can make it run their code inherits its admin key without touching the console
At the developer's laptop only, since pipelines cannot be attacked
Nowhere: MFA on the console protects every path into the account
explain: Console MFA protects one door. The pipeline is another identity with the same or more power, and it acts on code it is given. Controlling its input or its runner is as good as owning its key.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: CircleCI 2023: when the platform holding your secrets is breached
question: CircleCI encrypted customer secrets at rest. Why were they still exposed?
options: The encryption algorithm was broken
The attacker extracted the encryption keys from a running process, which must hold them to use the secrets
Secrets were stored in plain text by mistake
The customers' own laptops were compromised
explain: The report says data was encrypted at rest but keys were extracted from a running process. At-rest encryption protects stolen disks and backups, not a service that is running and compromised.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Terraform state: the file that holds every secret
question: A team marks every secret variable `sensitive = true` and says their state is now safe to share with all engineers. What is wrong?
options: sensitive only redacts CLI and UI output; the values are still in the state file in plain text
Nothing: sensitive values are encrypted in state
sensitive deletes the values after apply
State files never contain variables
explain: The real run shows the password twice in terraform.tfstate. To keep a value out of state you need ephemeral values or write-only arguments, or a secret manager referenced at runtime.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: Drift detection: when the cloud stops matching the code
question: A scheduled `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` on main returns 2. Nobody merged anything since the last apply. What does it most likely mean?
options: Terraform crashed
No changes are needed
Something changed outside Terraform: drift that the owners must review
The state file is encrypted
explain: Exit code 2 means the plan succeeded and has changes. With no new code, those changes come from the live side: drift. Exit code 1 would be an error.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: The forward process: masking as noise, and its exact reverse
question: In a reverse step from t to s, a masked position stays masked with probability s/t. What happens when s = 0?
options: Every masked position is revealed in this step
Nothing is revealed, because s/t = 0 means no change
Half of the masked positions are revealed
The visible tokens are remasked
explain: With s = 0 the probability of staying masked is 0/t = 0, so every remaining mask must be filled. The last step of any schedule ends at s = 0 and finishes the sequence.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Where diffusion LMs stand: results, block diffusion, and limits
question: A team needs exact KV caching and variable-length outputs but wants some parallel decoding. Which design fits best?
options: Pure masked diffusion over a fixed 1024-token canvas
BERT with a 15% masking ratio
An autoregressive model sampled at high temperature
Block diffusion with a small block size, autoregressive across blocks
explain: Block diffusion freezes finished blocks, so their keys and values are cached exactly and generation can continue block after block. Diffusion inside each block still commits several tokens per pass. A fixed canvas has neither property, and BERT cannot sample text.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Splitting the phases: pools, ratios and parallelism
question: Using DistServe's equations with D = 0.1 s and K = 1.6, which 2-GPU plan gives lower average TTFT at a low arrival rate of 2 req/s?
options: Intra-op (tensor): it cuts execution time to D/K, and queueing is small at low rate
Neither; one GPU is always better
Inter-op (pipeline): it doubles capacity
They are identical at low rate
explain: At R = 2 the intra-op TTFT is 0.0625 + 0.0045 = about 0.067 s, while inter-op is 0.1 + 0.0028 = about 0.103 s. Execution time dominates at low load, so cutting it wins. At high load the queueing term flips the order.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Disaggregation at scale: MoE, expert parallelism and elastic pools
question: In a ping-pong pipeline, attention and FFN each take 2 ms per micro-batch and a one-way transfer takes 1 ms. What is the smallest number of micro-batches that keeps both sides busy?
explain: The condition is m x Tf at least 2(Tf + Tc): 2m at least 6, so m = 3. With 2, the attention GPUs idle 2 ms per layer waiting for a micro-batch to come back, as in the first scene of the timeline. More micro-batches also work but shrink each one, which lowers the per-expert batch.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: NTFS and the master file table, record by record
question: Record 812 is marked free and its sequence number is 4. An entry in the NTFS change journal (lesson 6) refers to file reference 812 with sequence 3. What does that tell you?
options: The journal entry describes the same file that the record holds now
The journal is corrupt, because sequence numbers never change
Record 812 is a directory
The journal entry describes an earlier file that used record 812 before it was freed
explain: The sequence number increments each time a record is freed. Sequence 3 in the reference versus 4 in the record means the record has been freed since; the reference points to an older occupant.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: APFS: containers, copy-on-write and snapshots
question: You remove the internal SSD from an Apple silicon Mac with FileVault on and image it with a write-blocker. What do you have?
options: A readable APFS volume, because write-blockers bypass encryption
Encrypted data that stays unreadable without valid credentials or a recovery key
A blank image, because the SSD erases itself
A readable image as long as you image the whole container
explain: Apple documents that internal APFS volumes stay encrypted without valid login credentials or a cryptographic recovery key, even attached to another computer. A write-blocker preserves data; it does not decrypt it.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: SRUM and browser history: network use and what was visited
question: The suspect cleared their browser history. What can SRUM still offer?
options: Per-application, per-user network byte counts with timestamps, showing that the browser moved data
The URLs that were visited
The content of the uploaded file
Nothing, because clearing history also clears SRUM
explain: SRUM's Network Usage table records BytesSent and BytesRecvd per application and user. It does not record URLs or content, and the browser's clear-history function does not touch SRUDB.dat.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Trusting your tools: Cellebrite, Signal (2021) and validation
question: Which practice most directly addresses the risk that one tool misparses a crucial artefact?
options: Running the same tool twice
Using a newer computer
Hashing the report
Confirming the finding with an independent tool and against the raw data
explain: A second, independent implementation is unlikely to share the first tool's bug, and checking the raw bytes removes tool interpretation. Running the same tool repeats the same error; hashing the report only shows it did not change later.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: Beyond beam search: SSD page layout and I/O efficiency
question: One billion 96-d float32 points, 32-byte PQ codes, R = 64. Using the repository's formula, what search RAM budget B should you pass?
options: About 3.2 GB
About 384 GB, the size of the full vectors
About 30 GB: 29.80 for the PQ codes plus 0.15 for the 250,000-node cache
About 0.15 GB, since only the cache lives in RAM
explain: n b / 2^30 = 10^9 x 32 / 2^30 = 29.80 GB for the codes. The cache term is 250,000 x (4 x 64 + 4 x 96) / 2^30 = 0.15 GB. Full vectors stay on the SSD; about 3.1 GB (2.98 + 0.15) would be the answer for 100M such points.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: CAGRA search on the GPU, and picking an index
question: A recommendation service sends one query at a time to a GPU CAGRA index, and the GPU is mostly idle. Which setting addresses this?
options: Multi-CTA search, which spreads one query across several thread blocks
A larger team_size
A smaller graph_degree
Single-CTA with a persistent kernel
explain: Single-CTA maps a query to one block, so a batch of 1 uses a sliver of the GPU. Multi-CTA assigns several CTAs to one query, each expanding a parent, which the paper designed for batch sizes of about 1 to 100. cuVS AUTO selects it for small batches.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: When preferences look certain: DPO overfits, IPO holds
question: With IPO at $\tau = 0.25$ in the two-answer toy, what probability does the policy converge to on $y_1$?
options: 50%, the reference
About 73%
About 88%
explain: The target gap is $1/(2\tau) = 2$, so $\pi(y_1) = \sigma(2) \approx 0.881$. Smaller $\tau$ means a bigger target gap and a more confident policy, but never fully deterministic.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Offline or on-policy: online DPO, and when RL still wins
question: A team runs offline DPO on pairs collected from GPT-4 and a few open models. Training accuracy hits 100%, but the model's own outputs got worse. Which change most directly targets the cause?
options: Increase beta so the policy stays closer to the reference
Switch to SimPO to drop the reference model
Sample pairs from the current policy, label them with a judge, and train again in rounds or online
Train for more epochs until the margin saturates
explain: The pairs describe other models' answers, so the loss says little about what this policy generates (the coverage problem). On-policy pairs, per round as in Llama 3 or per step as in OAIF, put the training signal where the policy actually puts probability. A larger beta slows drift but does not cover new outputs.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Backfilling history without overwriting newer writes
question: In DBLog, why drop a chunk row whose key changed inside the window, rather than keep the chunk's value?
options: The chunk value is always older than the log event
The select's exact log position is unknown, so its value may be older than the event; the event is at least as new, so emitting it alone is always safe
Dropping rows makes chunks smaller and faster to emit
Log events contain more columns than chunk rows
explain: The select happened somewhere inside the window, so for a key changed in the window it may have read the value before or after that change. Keeping the log event, which is the latest committed change for that key up to that point, is correct either way; keeping the chunk row could reintroduce an older value.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: X3DH step by step: four Diffie-Hellman results, one key
question: No one-time prekeys are left on the server for Bob. What changes?
options: DH4 is omitted; forward secrecy of that SK now rests on the signed prekey's lifetime
The protocol fails and Alice cannot message Bob
Alice reuses an old one-time prekey
The server generates a one-time prekey for Bob
explain: The spec computes SK = KDF(DH1 || DH2 || DH3) when no OPK exists. Until Bob deletes the SPK private key (after rotation), stealing IKB and SPKB would reveal that SK. Rotating signed prekeys often limits the window.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: The DH ratchet: healing after a key theft
question: Why does the Double Ratchet heal after a compromise while the symmetric ratchet alone does not?
options: HMAC is replaced by SHA-512
The server resets keys every hour
Each DH ratchet step mixes a DH output from freshly generated keys into the root key, which a past thief cannot compute
Messages are signed
explain: A symmetric chain is deterministic from the stolen chain key. The DH ratchet injects new secret input every round trip; without the new private keys, the thief cannot follow the root chain.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Key transparency: from CONIKS to WhatsApp and iMessage
question: Why does WhatsApp still recommend manual security-code checks to users who want the strongest assurance?
options: Automatic KT still relies on WhatsApp's directory and audit process; a manual out-of-band comparison needs no trust in WhatsApp's servers at all
Key transparency is not deployed
Manual checks are post-quantum
Codes encrypt messages
explain: The post says users who want to verify sessions "without utilizing WhatsApp servers at all" should keep using the traditional security code check. KT raises the bar and scales, but its checks still flow through the provider's infrastructure.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: MLS in practice: proposals, commits, epochs and the two services
question: A member lost their phone, which held their MLS state. What should happen in the group?
options: Nothing; the epoch secret expires daily
Change the group name
Remove that leaf (or have the member re-join and update) in a new Commit so later epochs use secrets the lost device cannot derive
Ask the DS to delete old messages
explain: The lost device knows the current epoch's secrets and its path keys. A Commit that removes or replaces its leaf, with a fresh path, gives post-compromise security; earlier epochs stay protected by forward secrecy once keys are deleted.

courseTitle: End-to-end encrypted messaging: Signal protocol and MLS
lessonTitle: Telegram's MTProto, and why messengers need proofs
question: A vendor says its new messenger protocol is secure because it uses only libsodium primitives. What is the strongest response?
options: Libsodium is outdated
Ask which AES key size it uses
Secure primitives do not make a secure protocol; ask for a published specification and a security analysis, ideally machine-checked, of the protocol itself
Accept it; libraries cannot be misused
explain: Threema used NaCl (a well-reviewed crypto library; libsodium is its fork) and Telegram used standard primitives; the breaks were in how they were composed. The Threema authors extend the mantra to "don't roll your own cryptographic protocol".

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
question: You need per-process counts of 2 million syscalls per second. Which bpftrace action is cheapest?
options: printf the process name on every event and count lines with sort and uniq -c
Write each event to a file with system()
They cost the same, since all run in the kernel
@[comm] = count(), printed once at exit
explain: count() updates a map inside the kernel, so nothing crosses to user space per event. printf sends a record per event that user space must read and format, which is far more work at millions of events per second.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
question: You need to know where CPU time goes in a busy service, across all functions, for 30 seconds in production. Which approach fits best?
options: kprobe on every kernel function with kprobe:* and count()
profile:hz:99 { @[kstack] = count(); } and render the result as a flame graph
printf the stack on every sched_switch
uprobe on every function in the binary
explain: Sampling at 99 Hz costs about 99 probe hits per CPU per second regardless of how busy the service is, and kstack keys give a frequency count of stacks for a flame graph. Probing every function makes the cost scale with the call rate, which can be enormous.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Integer-only inference: int8 multiplies, int32 accumulators
question: Why is the bias quantized to int32 with scale S1 x S2 instead of int8 with its own scale?
options: So it can be added directly into the int32 accumulator, and so its error does not become a systematic shift on every output
Because biases are larger than weights
Because int8 cannot represent negative biases
Because the bias is applied after dequantization to float
explain: The accumulator's scale is S1 x S2, so a bias at that scale is added with no conversion. Each bias value is added to many outputs, so any rounding error in it is a nonzero-mean error; 32 bits make it negligible, and biases are a tiny fraction of parameters.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Why appliances are hard to defend: patches, logs and trust
question: A NetScaler writes about 5 lines per second of roughly 300 bytes, with the default 2.5 MB of local logs, and nothing is forwarded. Investigators arrive the next morning. What history is on the box?
options: About the last half hour; older lines have rotated away
The last 90 days
Everything since the last reboot
Nothing; NetScaler does not log at all
explain: 2,500,000 / (5 x 300) is about 1,667 seconds, roughly 28 minutes. Without forwarding to a SIEM, the night's activity is gone. Mandiant warned exactly this for Citrix Bleed investigations.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: PAN-OS GlobalProtect, 2024: a cookie that became a command
question: Which single change would have stopped the first step of CVE-2024-3400, file creation from the cookie?
options: Disabling the web console
Running the telemetry job less often
Checking that the session ID is a valid UUID before using it in a file name
Using HTTPS instead of HTTP
explain: The first step needed path characters in the cookie to end up in a file name. A strict UUID check rejects them; that is the check Palo Alto's patch added. The shell=True fix stops the second step.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Detecting a compromised appliance from the outside
question: Which single signal is the strongest sign that an edge appliance itself is compromised?
options: A failed VPN login from a user who mistyped a password
The appliance starting a direct-to-IP download from an address it has never contacted
High CPU during business hours
A user connecting from home
explain: Appliances have short, predictable lists of destinations. Suspect traffic from the firewall itself was Volexity's first signal in the PAN-OS case, and direct-to-IP downloads from the device were a pattern it saw only from the attacker. The other options are everyday events.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Measuring wasted tokens and training them away
question: A team builds DPO pairs from a reasoning model's samples. Which pairing best matches what Chen et al. found effective?
options: Chosen: greedy response. Rejected: a random wrong response
Chosen: the longest correct response. Rejected: the shortest one
Chosen: a correct response trimmed to its first correct solution plus one reflection. Rejected: the longest sampled response
Chosen: a response from a non-reasoning model. Rejected: any reasoning-model response
explain: The positive is a streamlined trace from the model itself, so it stays in-distribution; the negative is the longest sample, which gave a clearer contrast than the greedy response.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Underthinking and early exit: stopping at the right moment
question: A model's wrong AIME answers look like this: a sound approach in the first 400 tokens, then 15 'Alternatively' switches and 8,000 tokens with no conclusion. Which training-free change targets this failure directly?
options: DEER early exit at threshold 0.95
A smaller max_output_tokens cap
A thought-switching penalty on 'Alternatively' during the first few hundred tokens of each thought
Self-consistency over 4 samples of the same model
explain: This is underthinking: the first idea was right but abandoned. TIP makes the model develop each idea longer before switching. DEER helps when a confident answer already exists; a cap just truncates; voting can help but does not change how each trace reasons.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Many spellings of one value: UTF-8 overlongs and base64 slack
question: Your API rejects a list of known-bad base64 tokens by comparing the token text, then decodes and uses the bytes. What is the most robust fix?
options: Also block the token with `==` appended
Decode strictly (reject junk and non-zero pad bits), then compare the decoded bytes
Lower-case tokens before comparing
Switch to hex encoding
explain: Many strings can decode to the same bytes (non-zero pad bits, ignored junk characters). Comparing the decoded bytes, after a strict decode, makes the decision on the value you will use. Adding variants one at a time never ends.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Case mapping and case folding: when lower() is not one-to-one
question: In Django's CVE-2019-19844 fix, why send the reset email to the stored address rather than the submitted one?
options: Stored addresses are already lower-case, so mail delivery is faster
The submitted address might contain spaces
It guarantees the token reaches the account's real owner even if the matching step is fooled
SMTP servers reject Unicode addresses
explain: The matching logic decides which account the token is for; the delivery address decides who receives it. Tying delivery to the stored address means a matching bug can at worst send the owner an unexpected email.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Internationalised domain names, Punycode and what browsers show
question: Why did Chrome's 2017 mixed-script rule fail against `аррӏе.com`?
options: Chrome did not support Punycode
The letters were fullwidth
The domain used a Cyrillic TLD
The label was entirely Cyrillic, so it was not mixed-script: a whole-script confusable
explain: Mixed-script rules catch Latin plus Cyrillic in one label. A label written only in Cyrillic lookalikes is single-script, so it needs a whole-script confusable check, which Chrome added.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: XML, multipart forms and email addresses: same bytes, different trees
question: A fraud service reads the first `amount` field of a multipart body and the payment service reads the last. What is the right fix?
options: Reject requests where a single-value field appears more than once, at the first parser, and forward the parsed values
Make the fraud service read the last value too
Limit the body size
Encode amounts in base64
explain: Aligning the two services by convention works until one library changes. Rejecting the ambiguity at the edge means both services receive one unambiguous value.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Where a sensor sits: kernel callbacks, minifilters and network filters
question: A sensor driver wants to stop `invoice.exe` from ever running. Where can it do that?
options: In a post-operation file minifilter callback after the EXE is closed
In its process-creation callback, by setting CreationStatus to an error code
In the WFP network filter when the process first connects
In the console, once the alert arrives
explain: The process-creation callback runs before the new process starts, and the documented CreationStatus field lets the driver fail the creation. A network filter or console action can only act after the process is already running.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Worked configs: SwiftOnSecurity's sysmon-config and sysmon-modular
question: A sysmon-modular coverage layer shows ATT&CK technique T1055 as 'covered'. What can you conclude?
options: Every process injection on these hosts will be detected
Defender for Endpoint is no longer needed
T1055 events are now blocked
The config collects telemetry that may be useful for T1055; whether it records a given implementation, and whether any detection rule uses it, still needs testing
explain: The project's README states that ATT&CK mappings identify potentially useful telemetry and do not guarantee that every implementation is recorded or that a detection exists. Coverage of data is not coverage of detection.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control II: App Control for Business, drivers and LOLBins
question: Your App Control policy runs in enforce mode and you see a 3076 event on one laptop. What does that tell you?
options: The file was blocked
The policy failed to load
The file was allowed by the ISG
That laptop is still running an audit-mode policy (or an additional audit policy), because 3076 is the audit-mode would-be block
explain: 3076 is written only for audit-mode policies; enforced blocks are 3077. A 3076 on a machine you believe is enforced means a policy there is in audit mode, which is worth checking with CiTool -lp and event 3099.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Tampering and EDR killers: SUNBURST, BYOVD and AuKill
question: Which control stops AuKill's outdated Process Explorer driver from loading if the file is already on disk?
options: The ASR rule 'Block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers'
Sysmon event 6
LAPS
The vulnerable driver blocklist or an App Control driver block policy
explain: Microsoft's ASR reference says that rule prevents writing vulnerable signed drivers but does not stop an existing driver from loading; the blocklist or App Control policy prevents the load. Sysmon only records; LAPS manages passwords.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Running edge detection and ON/OFF matching on the toy house
question: Which change to the toy pipeline would most directly avoid the minute-45 failure?
options: Raise the edge threshold from 30 W to 70 W
Use more clusters in k-means
Sample faster so the lamp-off and fridge-on events fall in different samples
Use the cluster median instead of the mean as each appliance's power
explain: The failure comes from two events sharing one sample. Faster sampling separates them into two clean edges (-60 then +120). A 70 W threshold would drop the +64 edge but also the lamp's real +51 ON edge, and the fridge would still have no ON edge at 45. More clusters or a median do not undo a merged edge.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Cleaning: Unicode, case, punctuation and legal suffixes
question: Which single step makes `Ｑｕａｎｔｉｘ` (full-width) equal to `Quantix`?
options: Case folding with casefold()
Unicode NFC normalization
Unicode NFKC normalization
Removing punctuation
explain: Full-width letters are compatibility characters. Only the K forms (NFKD, NFKC) apply compatibility mappings; NFC handles canonical equivalence only and leaves them unchanged. Case folding does not map full-width letters to ASCII.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Learned matchers: active learning, classifiers and language models
question: You have 50 labelled pairs and 10 million candidate pairs after blocking, and must score them all nightly on CPUs. Which matcher fits best?
options: A zero-shot LLM on every candidate pair
Ditto fine-tuned on the 50 labels
A regularized logistic regression on field-comparison features, with active learning to spend new labels well, and an LLM only for the uncertain band
Exact string equality, because it needs no labels
explain: At about USD 60 per million pairs even the cheapest LLM in the paper costs about USD 600 per night for 10 million pairs, and its requests take over a second each. Ditto needs thousands of labels. A classifier on comparison features learns from few labels and scores millions of pairs in seconds on a CPU; the LLM can still judge the few hundred pairs it is unsure about.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
question: A raw title `Sr SDET` must map to an O*NET code. Which pipeline gets it right in the computed example?
options: Embed the raw string and take the nearest occupation name
Lowercase, then exact lookup in the occupation names
Expand abbreviations, strip seniority, then match against occupation names plus alternate titles
Strip seniority only, then embed and take the nearest occupation name
explain: Raw abbreviations score near noise (`SDET` peaks at 0.25), and an exact lookup never finds `sr sdet`. Even after expansion, the occupation name alone picks Software Developers (0.68 vs 0.60). Matching against reported titles such as Software Test Engineer gives the testers occupation at 0.92.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: App registrations vs service principals: how an app gets an identity
question: Which audit activity best catches someone quietly taking over an existing powerful app in your tenant?
options: Update application - Certificates and secrets management (or Add service principal credentials)
Add user
Consent to application
Register device
explain: Taking over an existing app means adding a credential to it, which logs as a certificates and secrets update on the application or added service principal credentials. Consent and new users are other steps of other patterns.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Device code phishing: Storm-2372 and signing in for someone else
question: A tenant blocks device code flow everywhere except for the SharePoint resource. A user's session began with a device code sign-in to SharePoint. They then try to open Exchange Online in the same session. What does Microsoft document?
options: Exchange is blocked, because the session is protocol tracked and the device code policy applies to later requests from it
Exchange is allowed because the user signed in normally
Exchange prompts for a new device code
The policy is ignored for refresh tokens
explain: Microsoft's example is exactly this: protocol tracking keeps the session marked as device code through later refreshes, so a sign-in to Exchange in that session is blocked by the authentication flows policy.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Hybrid identity: Entra Connect, PTA, Seamless SSO and Tier 0
question: Why does Microsoft recommend rolling the AZUREADSSOACC Kerberos decryption key at least every 30 days?
options: Because anyone holding a copy of that key can create tickets Entra ID trusts for synced users, so a regular rollover limits how long a stolen copy stays useful
Because Kerberos tickets expire after 30 days
To change the encryption from AES to RC4
Because the key is needed to sync passwords
explain: Entra ID decrypts Seamless SSO tickets with that key, so a stolen copy works like a silver ticket key for the cloud sign-in. Rolling it regularly, and after any AD compromise, retires old copies.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
question: Why do event loops set O_NONBLOCK on every socket even though they only read sockets the kernel reported as ready?
options: Because epoll refuses to watch blocking sockets
Because nonblocking reads are faster to copy
Because readiness can be spurious, and one blocking read would stall every other client on the loop
Because blocking sockets cannot be written to
explain: epoll watches blocking sockets just fine. But a readiness report is only a hint: the data may have been discarded, or another thread may have consumed it. With a blocking socket that read would put the only loop thread to sleep, and every other connection would wait with it.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Event loops in practice: libuv, timers, thread pools
question: The only active timer is due in 250 ms, no idle handles are active and nothing is closing. What timeout does libuv pass to the poll step?
options: 0, so it can check the timer often
-1 (infinite), since timers are handled separately
250 ms: sleep until the nearest timer is due unless I/O arrives first
10 ms, a fixed tick
explain: The libuv rules give 0 only when the loop is stopping, has nothing active, has idle handles, or is closing handles. Otherwise the timeout is the time until the closest timer, and infinity only when there are no timers. The I/O wait and the timer wait are one blocking call.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Testing many variants: Bonferroni and Holm corrections
question: Why did the 17 null variants in the concrete run look better than the baseline on average?
options: The paired t-test is biased toward the variant
Every comparison reused the same baseline run, which happened to score low on these queries, so the tests are correlated
Holm correction shifts p-values downward
The variants were trained on the test queries
explain: The baseline scored 0.357 while its true quality is 0.402. Every variant was compared to that one unlucky draw, so they all looked better together. Shared baselines make multiple tests correlated, which is why the observed FWER (0.421) differs from the independence formula (0.642).

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Why attackers then reuse existing code
question: Why did NX alone not end memory-corruption exploits?
options: Because NX can be turned off by any program
Because NX only applies to 32-bit processes
Because NX leaks the canary
Because attackers could still redirect control to code that is already executable, such as functions and instruction sequences in libc
explain: NX blocks running data as code, but a hijacked return or function pointer can target existing executable code. That is the core insight of return-into-libc and of Shacham's return-oriented programming paper.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Protecting returns: shadow stacks and pointer authentication
question: An overflow writes past a buffer using an index, skipping the canary and changing only the saved return address. Which mitigation still catches it at return?
options: A hardware shadow stack, because it compares the return address itself with a protected copy
The stack canary
FORTIFY_SOURCE
Partial RELRO
explain: The canary is untouched, so its check passes. The shadow stack compares the actual return address with a copy that normal stores cannot change, so any modification is caught.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: Turning mitigations on and checking a binary
question: `readelf -lW prog` shows a GNU_RELRO segment, and `readelf -d prog` shows `FLAGS_1 PIE` but no BIND_NOW or NOW flag. What should you conclude?
options: Partial RELRO and PIE: .got.plt is still writable; add -Wl,-z,now
Full RELRO and PIE
No RELRO, because BIND_NOW is missing
Not PIE, because BIND_NOW is missing
explain: GNU_RELRO alone is partial RELRO. Full RELRO also needs immediate binding (BIND_NOW / NOW). PIE is indicated separately by the PIE flag and the DYN file type.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Putting a price on the ping-pong
question: Under the model with h = 1, C = 100 and b = 50, what is the slowdown S for 8 threads sharing one line?
explain: S = k(1 + C/(b h)) = 8 x (1 + 100/50) = 8 x 3 = 24. The 808 answer is the b = 1 worst case, and 3 forgets to multiply by k: all k threads' writes go through one line, one at a time.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
question: Client A (54 examples) returns 0.10, client B (36) returns 0.80, client C (18) returns 2.70, but this round client B drops out and never reports. What does FedAvg set as the new global model?
options: 0.767, since the weights 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108 are properties of the clients
0.500, the weighted average with client B's contribution set to zero
0.750, the weighted average of A and C renormalized over 72 examples
The round is discarded, because FedAvg requires every selected client
explain: The denominator is m_t, the examples in this round only: 54 + 18 = 72. So the model is (54/72) x 0.10 + (18/72) x 2.70 = 0.075 + 0.675 = 0.750. Keeping stale weights that sum to less than one (option B) would shrink the model toward zero, and single dropouts never abandon a round.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
question: Why is SCAFFOLD usually described as a better fit for cross-silo than for cross-device federated learning?
options: It requires every client to keep its control variate across rounds and doubles the upload, while phones are stateless and rarely selected twice
It needs a GPU on every client
Its server update is incompatible with weighted averaging
It only converges when every client holds IID data
explain: The variate c_i is per-client state carried from one participation to the next, and the upload carries a model delta plus a variate delta. Ten hospitals that join every round can do both; a phone that participates once in a training run never gets to use its variate.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: What the server sees: secure aggregation and differential privacy
question: Why did Gboard's production training move from DP-FedAvg's accounting to DP-FTRL?
options: DP-FTRL needs no clipping
DP-FTRL does not add noise, so accuracy is higher
Secure aggregation cannot be used with DP-FedAvg
DP-FedAvg's best guarantees rely on amplification by sampling, which needs uniformly random client selection that a device fleet cannot guarantee
explain: Devices are eligible only when idle, charging and on an unmetered network, so the server cannot sample users uniformly, and the sampling-based accountant's assumption breaks. DP-FTRL adds tree-correlated noise to prefix sums of updates and gets its guarantee from bounding how often and how close together a client participates.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time
question: In the codetrace, why is J returned even though J is not in H's stored list?
options: J is H's entry point on the level
J was recovered from H's compressed M_beta entries
Truncation to M adds the next closest node
The lookup reads failing neighbor G's list and J passes the predicate
explain: ACORN-1 expands every neighbor u of H, including ones that fail, into u's own list, then filters. G fails but links to J, so J appears. There is no M_beta compression in ACORN-1 (it is fixed at M_beta = M).

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Shared experts: an always-on path for common knowledge
question: In the 2B ablation, removing the shared expert and activating one extra routed expert kept FLOPs equal but raised Pile loss from 1.808 to 2.414. What is the best reading?
options: The routed experts were undertrained, so any extra routed expert would hurt
The shared expert had learned common knowledge that the specialized routed experts do not hold, so it is not interchangeable with a routed one
Shared experts are larger than routed experts, so removing one removes compute
The loss rose because the router softmax had one fewer output
explain: Both configurations use the same number and size of active experts. The jump shows the shared expert holds something the routed experts never learned because they could rely on it: the common knowledge the design meant to isolate.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: Build it: a DeepSeekMoE layer with bias balancing in your GPT
question: Where must `update_bias` run relative to the training step?
options: Before the forward pass, using the counts the forward pass will produce
Inside the loss, so autograd can adjust it
After `opt.step()`, under `torch.no_grad()`, using the counts recorded by this step's forward pass, and before an evaluation pass overwrites them
Only at the end of training, once
explain: Algorithm 1 adjusts the bias from the load just observed, outside the gradient computation. Running it inside autograd would make it a learned parameter (and leak balance into the loss), and running it after an eval forward would balance the wrong batch. Counts from the current step only steer the next step's routing, so no future token leaks.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Secure Boot keys: PK, KEK, db and dbx
question: An attacker obtains the private key of one KEK enrolled on a fleet of laptops, but not the PK. What can they do?
options: Nothing, only the PK matters
Replace the PK
Sign db and dbx updates, for example adding their own certificate to db
Read the TPM's private keys
explain: Per the UEFI spec, db and dbx updates must be signed by a KEK or the PK. A KEK holder can therefore add an allowed certificate. Replacing the PK needs the PK private key.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: The 2023 to 2026 Microsoft certificate rollover
question: Why did Microsoft add the PCA 2011 certificate to dbx instead of continuing to add hashes of vulnerable boot managers?
options: Listing every vulnerable boot manager by hash was unreliable and costly; revoking the CA distrusts all of them at once
Hashes cannot be stored in dbx
The certificate had already expired
To free space in db
explain: Hash revocation misses rebuilds and consumes dbx space. Distrusting the signing certificate catches every boot manager it signed, at the cost of requiring a newly signed boot manager and updated media.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Hardware roots of trust: Boot Guard, AMD PSB and Apple silicon
